purpose: Compare the complete CUDA and SYCL calls of the three workloads on one RTX 4090, built and run in one WSL distro so that both share the host, the driver and the path to the GPU

amendment.replaces: the protocol committed in 92179878456986940d6e60a6c87b726a80edb775, under which no sample was taken
amendment.reason: the card never fell under 10 percent utilization in 229 readings from 2026-11-16 to 2026-11-22 with no game running, so I decided that the run goes ahead at the usual desktop load, with CUDA and SYCL alternating back to back many times, the card's utilization and memory recorded with every sample and the results labeled as measured on a working desktop with that load stated
changes: the 10 percent precondition gives way to the usual desktop load with no game running
CUDA and SYCL calls of one workload run as back to back pairs, with the first backend alternating between iterations
121 samples per condition in place of 25
an NVML reading of utilization and memory before every recorded call, and idle readings before each side and after the last one
the summary adds the median of the paired ratios and the load
the time limit rises from 120 to 600 seconds

preconditions: source and protocol committed before collection
the native, cuda_ and sycl_ tests and --verify passed with the same build on the measuring computer
no game running, checked privately by the person who starts the run, while the usual desktop applications keep using the GPU and their load is recorded with every sample
no other build, benchmark or test job running on the computer, which heavy.lock arranges between the repositories on it
histogram_bins: block shared bins for CUDA and work group local bins for SYCL, the default of each call
launch_shape: both libraries use blocks or work groups of 256, one for each tile in the histogram, and at most 4096 for the stencil and the first reduction pass, with a second reduction pass of one block or work group, as src/cuda.cu and src/sycl.cpp fix it and tests/python/test_sycl_cuda_plan.py checks
inputs: values i modulo 1009 divided by 1009 minus 0.5, mask true unless i is a multiple of 3, image byte i times 13 modulo 256, the inputs of docs/pinned-protocol.json
host_memory: pageable vectors for every input, and outputs that each library allocates and returns
first_sample: iteration zero is one of the 121 retained rows of each condition, reported apart from the 120 warm samples that the summary uses. The first call of each backend in the process, which may load its device code, falls in iteration zero of the first side, so it is not a warm measurement and not a cold process measurement
order: for iteration k and side index c, run position p from 0 to 5 holds workload (k+c+floor(p/2)) modulo three and backend (p+k) modulo two, with CUDA as backend 0. Each workload thus runs as a CUDA call and a SYCL call back to back, CUDA first in even iterations and SYCL first in odd ones, and over any six iterations each workload holds each place in the round with each backend first exactly once, so the 120 warm iterations hold each arrangement 20 times. Two additional warmup rounds of the six combinations follow iteration zero
pairs: the CUDA row and the SYCL row of one side, workload and iteration form a pair, and the ratio of their complete calls is taken within the pair, so that both calls share nearly the same background load
gpu_readings: before each recorded call, outside host timing, hbr_sycl_cuda_bench reads the card through NVML, which it opens at run time and finds by the UUID of the CUDA device. gpu_util_percent is the percent of the last NVML sample period, between 1/6 and 1 second, in which any kernel of any process ran, so it includes kernels of this benchmark's earlier calls as well as the desktop's. gpu_memory_mib is the memory all processes hold on the card. Before each side and after the last one, a pause of 2 seconds with no call from this process precedes an idle reading, printed to stderr and kept in the receipt, which shows the desktop load alone. The GPU UUID is not printed
context: before any recorded row, hbr::cuda_device and cudaFree(nullptr) create the CUDA primary context, and hbr::sycl_device selects the GPU that every SYCL call selects. nm -D --undefined-only on lib/libur_adapter_cuda.so of the DPC++ 7.2.0 release lists cuDevicePrimaryCtxRetain and cuCtxSetCurrent and no cuCtxCreate, which points to both backends working in the same primary context. The run does not check that. Both benchmark modes stop before any sample when the two backends report different device names
host_timing: steady_clock from entry until the call returns an owned completed result, the same boundary for both backends, before comparison and destruction
cuda_call_includes: host result allocation for the histogram and the stencil, while the reduction returns a double
a device allocation call for each buffer
device memory release and event and stream destruction
sycl_call_includes: host result allocation for the histogram and the stencil, while the reduction returns a double
GPU selection among the GPUs that can run every kernel of the library, on every call
the fp64 or atomic64 check of the selected GPU
a device allocation call for each buffer
queue drain, device memory release and queue destruction before return
outside_host_timing: the NVML readings and idle pauses
device_timing: CUDA rows also record the library's upload, kernel and download events on its stream, never summed with host time. The SYCL library records no device events, so SYCL rows leave those fields empty, and only the complete call is compared across backends
correctness: every recorded and warmup output compared with the scalar CPU reference, exact for histogram counts, 1e-9 for the reduction and 1e-12 per stencil value, and every reduction and stencil output equal bit for bit to the first output of its backend, workload and side. --verify also reports whether the two backends give outputs equal bit for bit, as an observation and not a gate
summary: SYCL median divided by CUDA median for each condition
median and quartiles of the 120 paired SYCL to CUDA ratios for each side and workload, and their medians with CUDA first and with SYCL first
median and range of gpu_util_percent and gpu_memory_mib for each side, and the idle readings
build: one CMake build in the WSL distro HBR-SYCL-20261115 with HBR_CUDA and HBR_SYCL on, Release, the DPC++ 7.2.0 clang++ as the C++ compiler and linker, nvcc 13.2.86 with g++ as its host compiler, CUDA architecture 89 and the SYCL target nvidia_gpu_sm_89
scope: the complete synchronous calls of both libraries as they stand at the protocol commit, one call at a time in one process on one thread, with no runtime queue, no Python, no pinned memory, no device memory kept by either library between calls, whatever either runtime pools underneath, and no kernel only comparison for SYCL
environment: record CPU, GPU, driver, compilers, OS, WSL kernel, source, protocol and binary identities and GPU utilization, memory and temperature before and after in the receipt, have the person who starts the run check the GPU processes beforehand for a game and keep that list in a private record outside the repository, since the computer is a shared desktop, and preserve ordinary applications and default settings, which keep their load on the card during the run
decision: retain every result, including any where SYCL is slower, and report the CUDA and SYCL medians side by side for each condition. Label every published result as measured on a working desktop, with the load the readings show stated beside it. The result speaks for these three calls on this card under WSL at that load and makes no general claim about SYCL, CUDA, native Linux or an idle card
historical_evidence: leave the 504 original rows, the 900 reuse rows, the pinned protocol, their records and the cost model unchanged. Those CUDA runs were built with MSVC on Windows and are not comparable with the CUDA rows of this run
